title: What is physical AI? How Trainium accelerates how robots learn.
summary: For robots, a split-second delay can change the outcome. Here's why speed matters for physical AI, and how AWS Trainium helps.
body_markdown:
---


## Key takeaways


- Physical AI must sense, decide, and act in fractions of a second, unlike chatbots.


- [Inference speed](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-ceo-ai-inference-transforms-developer-capabilities) , not just training, determines whether a robot can work in real time.


- Runway cut robot wait time about fivefold on


[Trainium3](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/trainium-3-ultraserver-faster-ai-training-lower-cost) , fast enough to drive a robot live.


---


An object slips off a shelf, and a robot nearby has a fraction of a second to react. It needs to see the object falling, understand where it’s headed, and move to catch it. A delayed response could mean the difference between catching a falling object and watching it hit the floor. For a robot, how quickly it can think matters as much as how much it knows.


[Amazon uses robots that sort, lift, and carry packages—see them in action](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/operations/amazon-robotics-robots-fulfillment-center)


These nine robots help make employees' jobs safer and more productive by handling physically demanding tasks, freeing up time for skilled technical roles.


## Physical AI needs faster responses than chatbots


[Physical AI](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-physical-ai-toolchain-build-intelligent-machines) describes systems that perceive their surroundings, understand what’s happening, make decisions, and take action in the


[physical world](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/operations/amazon-vulcan-robot-pick-stow-touch) —a


[robot](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/tag/robotics) navigating an unfamiliar environment, a car responding to changing road conditions, or a machine learning to manipulate objects it has never encountered before.


A language model can take a moment to formulate a response without much consequence. A robot needs to continuously interpret information from cameras and sensors, understand how objects and people around it are moving, and decide what to do next, often in fractions of a second.


## Training vs. inference: how AI chips help robots learn and act


The capabilities of an AI model depend not only on its architecture and training data, but also on the computing infrastructure used to build and run it. Specialized AI chips such as


[AWS Trainium](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/why-ai-startups-choose-amazon-trainium-chips) play an important role at two stages: training and inference.


Training is the process through which a model learns from data, identifies patterns, and develops the capabilities it needs to perform a task. For physical AI, learning from examples is rarely enough. Demonstrations mostly show tasks going right, so a robot trained only by imitation can struggle to recover when something goes wrong. Robots also need to learn from experience.


That’s where reinforcement learning comes in. A robot practices a task over and over and improves from both its successes and its mistakes. Because real-world trial and error is slow and costly, much of this practice happens in simulation. Thousands of virtual robots can train in parallel before the skills they learn are transferred to physical machines.


Reinforcement learning also blurs the line between


[training](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/ai-chip-terms-explained) and


[inference](https://www.aboutamazon.com/stories/what-is-ai-inference-ai-agents) . The model runs repeatedly to generate experiences, then gets updated based on what it learned, and the cycle repeats. Faster, more efficient chips shorten every turn of that loop, creating a path for robots to improve faster and more efficiently.


Once a model is trained, it needs computing power to put what it has learned into practice. This is called inference: the process of running a trained model to interpret new information and generate a response. For physical AI, inference performance is especially important because the model needs to respond to its environment in real time.


One critical measure is latency, or the time it takes for a model to produce an answer. A robot that hesitates before making its next move may struggle to perform a task smoothly or safely. It needs to process information, make decisions, and act continuously.


[Inside a decade of Amazon chip design, built workload by workload](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/innovation-at-amazon/peter-desantis-amazon-ai-chips-design)


At AI Infra Summit, Amazon SVP Peter DeSantis explained how real customer workloads guided every generation of Amazon's chips, from Nitro to Trainium.


## Why the AI chip matters as much as the AI model


Think of it like a driver and a car. The driver represents the AI model: its ability to interpret a situation and decide what to do. The car represents the underlying computing hardware. Even a highly capable driver is limited by a car that can’t accelerate or respond quickly enough. Similarly, the performance of an AI model depends in part on the chips powering it.


As models increase their learning capacity by scaling up in size, they may need to distribute their workloads across multiple chips that must communicate quickly and efficiently. The speed of those connections, alongside the performance of each individual chip, can affect how quickly the entire system responds. More efficient computing can also help developers run more experiments, improve their models, and make physical AI applications more practical to deploy at scale.


## How Runway got a robot to respond in real time on Trainium


Runway’s robotics engineers worked with


[Annapurna Labs](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/take-a-look-inside-the-lab-where-aws-makes-custom-chips) (the team that designs Amazon’s AI chips) to run Praxis-1, a state-of-the-art world action model that learns from video data, on


[Trainium](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-trainium-graviton-ai-chips-explained) , with support from AWS Forward Deployed Engineering. Runway and Annapurna Labs collaborated to tune both the model and its low-level kernels. They cut the time the robot waits for its next move (per-chunk idle time) to 104 milliseconds on Trainium3, exceeding real-time metrics by more than 30% (Runway’s real-time target was 150 millisecond). Praxis-1 now runs on Trainium3 fast enough to drive a robot live, with room to spare, and it’s the top-performing world action model on NVIDIA’s RoboLab-120 leaderboard.


Part of Runway’s speedup came from using Trainium’s industry-leading performance profiler, which identifies performance opportunities at microsecond granularity. This tool, coupled with Trainium’s Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) and Trainium’s agentic tooling, meant Runway could find optimizations across the full stack. These included communication patterns between chips (known as a sharding strategy) and custom kernels written with NKI that tailor the model to Trainium.


[How DoorDash is using AWS to teach a delivery robot the rules of the road](https://www.aboutamazon.com/stories/doordash-aws-autonomous-delivery-robot)


DoorDash Labs engineers are using Amazon Web Services to pack all the capabilities of an autonomous car into a robot a fraction of the size.


## What’s next for physical AI and Amazon AI chips


Physical AI is still an emerging field, but its potential extends across industries and applications. As developers work to build models that can understand and interact with real-world environments, the computing infrastructure behind those models will play an increasingly important role.


Because Amazon designs Trainium, the engineers who built the chip can work directly with customers like Runway to tune it for their models. Advances in AI hardware, combined with collaboration between silicon designers and model developers, can help make these systems faster, more efficient, and more practical to deploy. With Trainium, Amazon is working to provide the specialized computing foundation developers need to push the boundaries of what’s possible with AI—not just in the digital world, but in the physical one, too.
